source_title: 5 Open-World RPGs That Basically Last Forever, Ranked
source_excerpt:
Open-world RPGs are some of the longest games around, with campaigns and side content often lasting upwards of 100 hours. However, in many of those cases, the game fundamentally comes to an end after all the loose story threads are wrapped up, and you have scoured every corner of the map for the last few items and collectibles.
However, in some cases, a game can effectively last forever , giving you an endless stream of content that never runs out so long as you are happy to keep pressing on. These next games achieve this through a replayable gameplay loop, smart use of AI, or by adopting such an open-ended design that no matter how many hours you sink into it, there will always be more to see.
Constant updates fill the game with content.
Camp expansion defines a lot of the gameplay.
Fallout 76 isn’t built to end because, much like any other live-service game, it is never truly finished. The post-apocalyptic wasteland has been updated nonstop since launch with new questlines, seasons, daily operations, public events, and expeditions that keep adding new goals to an already robust survival and gear crafting loop.
Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!
Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!
Recent patches like the Slasher update showcase this concept perfectly, adding a multi-week storyline alongside new items to chase that keep longtime players invested. Because content arrives continuously, there’s always another reason to log in. Now, almost a decade since launch, I am still amazed at just how much you can get out of a game that couldn't have had a rougher start.
Radiant quests keep generating new targets after the main story ends.
The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim’s secret to immortality is its Radiant quest system, which keeps generating new jobs after the main story is wrapped up. You might be sent to clear out a bandit camp, or a companion can direct you toward targets all across the land, and factions have their own specific quests that ensure your list is always filled to the brim.
Supplementing that stream of quests is the game's addictive loop for wandering around and stumbling upon adventure, which, thanks to the AI systems, can keep you roaming the world for literally thousands of hours. All of that without even mentioning mods, some of which add or convert large swaths of the experience into something entirely new. Even if Bethesda cut the story short, you can rest assured that the community will continue to pump out new things to do in Skyrim for years to come.
Constant shifts and reactions to enemies.
Mount & Blade 2: Bannerlord drops you into a lush medieval landscape as a nobody with nothing but a sword and a horse, and gives you no destination to chart a course for, but all the freedom to carve out your own story. From those humble beginnings, you begin to recruit troops that grow into armies , and a small camp of soldiers can transform into a castle-toppling force capable of taking over entire kingdoms, if you want them to.
The way the world is set up means you don't actually have to do anything for things to change. Lords change allegiances, kingdoms fall, and alliances break. There are always organic events breaking out in every region, extending a short play session into a several-hundred-hour experience that I truly believe has no equal in its genre.
Procedural Generation Means Infinite Possibilities
Every new character creates a different world.
Roguelikes are a breeding ground for endless content, and Caves of Qud is a rare example of an open-world RPG that fits perfectly into the genre. Each time you load in, the world is procedurally generated with villages and all manner of other structures and objects. That randomness extends to your character, who may begin with an extra limb or be adept at a specific skill, which alters the paths you take and how your run progresses.
The depth is borderline inexhaustible, mainly due to the many different combinations of items, enemies, and lore that all come together to create a wildly different feel across playthroughs. While there may be an actual ending to strive for, I would argue the real fun comes from going beyond it and seeking out any and all insane possibilities that the game is guaranteed to present you with.
Your reputation and outposts can keep expanding for as long as you want.
Rival factions keep the world unpredictable.
Kenshi intentionally sets its entry barriers high to show you exactly what kind of game it is. A sandbox in its purest form, you are driven by the desire to grow stronger, not by a narrative hook , and with no hands to hold along the way, a lot of your early hours will be spent scrambling to survive the brutal world around you.
Once you've gotten a grasp of the basics, Kenshi only becomes more open, as you attempt to fight back against enemies and stay at the top of the food chain. Yet no matter how many victories you achieve, there will always be raiders wandering around, waiting to attack your base, meaning you need to stay vigilant and ready for anything, no matter if you are 10 or 10,000 hours in. I think the brutality is what stops a lot of people from enjoying this game, but if you are willing to endure that hardship and push through, you will be treated to one of the most spectacular open-world RPGs ever made.
